original_value: This article reports on a novel higher-education course format exploiting choreographed peer reviews and self-corrections using an online learning platform. The novel course format aims to reduce teachers' workload   as it was motivated by the necessity to run examinations for all courses during all terms, even though almost all courses can only be offered every second term. As a consequence, and because of a very high students-to-teacher ratio, many students have to prepare for examinations without sufficient assistance. This article describes the novel course format and reports on its evaluation in a case study. The evaluation indicates that most students benefit from the novel course format but that it is less efficient than traditional formats based on a higher teachers' involvement. The major weakness of the novel format is the insufficient participation of some students to their peer-reviewing. The article suggests and discusses possible measures to address that weakness. This article extends previous work by the same authors by providing an extended evaluation of the students' attitudes towards the course format, their behavior on the platform and their peer reviews. The course format and the learning platform are described in greater detail and the integration into related work has been expanded.

result.paraphrase: This article presents a new higher-education course format that uses choreographed peer reviews and self-corrections on an online learning platform. It was designed to reduce teachers’ workload, driven by the need to hold examinations in all courses every term even though nearly all courses can be offered only every second term. Combined with a very high student-to-teacher ratio, this leaves many students to prepare for exams without enough support. The article outlines the format and evaluates it in a case study. The evaluation shows that most students benefit from the format, but it is less efficient than traditional formats with greater teacher involvement. Its main weakness is that some students do not participate sufficiently in peer review. The article also proposes and discusses measures to address this problem. It extends prior work by the same authors with a broader evaluation of students’ attitudes toward the format, their platform behavior, and their peer reviews, and it gives a more detailed description of the course format and learning platform while expanding the related-work integration.
